lessons.title: Name the three
lessons.objective: Name reason, purpose, and self-esteem as the three cardinal values, and say what cardinal means.

exercises.prompt: Which set is the three cardinal values in this ethics?

choices.text: Reason, purpose, and self-esteem
Faith, hope, and charity
Wealth, power, and duty
Feeling, habit, and sacrifice

feedback.note: The cardinal values are reason, purpose, and self-esteem. The other lists name substitutes or unrelated aims.

exercises.prompt: In this unit, what does cardinal mean?

choices.text: A primary value the rest of the code depends on
A rule issued by a church office
A minor taste one may drop without cost
A count of how many friends one has

feedback.note: Cardinal marks the values that come first. Lesser preferences hang from them; they do not replace them.

exercises.prompt: Match each cardinal value to the job it does.

pairs.left: Reason
pairs.right: The means of knowing what is true

pairs.left: Purpose
pairs.right: The chosen goal that ranks other values

pairs.left: Self-esteem
pairs.right: The conviction that one is able and worthy

feedback.note: Each value has a distinct job. Knowing, choosing a central goal, and trusting one's own mind are not the same task.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the three cardinal values.

feedback.note: Keep the set to reason, purpose, and self-esteem. Faith and sacrifice are not members of it.

exercises.prompt: Build the standard order of the three cardinal values.

feedback.note: The usual order is reason, then purpose, then self-esteem. Whim and sacrifice do not belong in the list.

exercises.prompt: Which item is not one of the three cardinal values?

choices.text: Drifting with the mood of the moment
Reason
Purpose
Self-esteem

feedback.note: Drifting is the absence of a chosen purpose, not a cardinal value beside the other three.

exercises.prompt: Match each substitute to the cardinal value it tries to replace.

pairs.left: Faith instead of evidence
Waiting to be assigned a life
A verdict borrowed from a crowd

feedback.note: Each substitute drops the value it mimics. Evidence, a chosen goal, and one's own judgment are what the substitutes leave out.

exercises.prompt: Why does this ethics name three cardinal values instead of a pile of likes?

choices.text: A human life needs these three at the root
Three is a fashionable number of hobbies
A statute requires every person to list three tastes
The count was chosen by chance

feedback.note: The three are cardinal because life as a thinking being depends on them, not because a list happened to be short.

exercises.prompt: Say what a cardinal value is, and what it is not.

feedback.note: Cardinal means primary. A passing preference can change without rewriting the code; these three cannot.

lessons.title: Reason as a value
lessons.objective: Explain reason as the cardinal value that makes knowledge and chosen action possible.

exercises.prompt: What is reason, as this unit uses the word?

choices.text: The faculty that identifies what is real
A mood that decides without evidence
Whatever most people currently feel
A voice that reveals facts without looking

feedback.note: Reason identifies reality. A mood, a vote, or a claimed revelation is not a substitute for that work.

exercises.prompt: Why is reason a value, and not only a description of a faculty?

choices.text: A person's life depends on knowing the facts
Clear speech is a pleasant style
Schools award points for long essays
Thinking is a habit one may skip with no loss

feedback.note: Reason is a value because survival and chosen action require knowledge. Skipping it is not a harmless style choice.

exercises.prompt: Match each act to using reason or refusing it.

pairs.left: Checking a claim against the facts
Acting on a wish that contradicts the facts
Revising a conclusion when the evidence changes

feedback.note: Using reason means staying with the facts, including when a conclusion has to change. A wish against the facts is a refusal.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about reason.

feedback.note: Reason is a faculty of identification. It does not invent reality, and a mood does not do its job.

exercises.prompt: Which claim treats feelings as a replacement for reason?

choices.text: If I feel it strongly, the facts must give way
A strong feeling is a clue I still have to check
I can name what I observe before I judge it
I change my mind when the evidence requires it

feedback.note: A feeling can be noticed. It does not outrank the facts. Treating it as a standard is a rejection of reason.

exercises.prompt: State what rejecting reason amounts to.

feedback.note: Rejecting reason does not sharpen sight or bend reality. It means acting as if the facts did not bind the choice.

exercises.prompt: Does reason create reality?

choices.text: No. It identifies what exists.
Yes. Thinking makes the facts whatever one prefers.
Only when a group agrees to create them.
Only when faith is added to the thought.

feedback.note: Reason is a means of knowing, not a power that decrees. The facts stay what they are whether or not one thinks well.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its meaning in this lesson.

pairs.left: Reason
Fact
Whim
pairs.right: A feeling treated as a standard

feedback.note: Reason answers to facts. A whim promotes a feeling into a standard and thereby drops that answer.

exercises.prompt: Why does this unit put reason first among the three cardinal values?

choices.text: Purpose and self-esteem depend on thinking
The word comes first in the alphabet
Thinking is easier than choosing a goal
Other people can see thoughts more easily than goals

feedback.note: Reason comes first because a purpose has to fit the facts, and self-esteem has to be about a mind that actually thinks.

lessons.title: Purpose
lessons.objective: Explain purpose as a chosen central goal that ranks a person's other values.

exercises.prompt: What is purpose, as a cardinal value?

choices.text: A chosen long-range goal that organizes one's life
Whatever one feels like doing this hour
A task assigned by someone else with no choice
A fate one discovers and must not question

feedback.note: A purpose is chosen and long-range. A mood, an imposed order, or an unquestioned fate is not that value.

exercises.prompt: What does this ethics treat as the central purpose of a rational person's life?

choices.text: Productive work
Avoiding every effort
Being noticed, whatever the work
Escaping the need to choose

feedback.note: Productive work is the central purpose. It is the goal that can integrate the rest of a life, not a substitute for one.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to the right label.

pairs.left: A chosen long-range goal
The central purpose of a rational life
A feeling that picks a new aim every hour

feedback.note: Purpose is the chosen goal. Productive work is the central case of it. A rotating mood never settles into a purpose.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about productive work.

feedback.note: Productive work is central purpose, not a side hobby and not an excuse for having no goal.

exercises.prompt: What does a purpose do to a person's other values?

choices.text: It ranks them so they form an order
It erases every value except one hobby
It freezes them so none can ever be reconsidered
It hides them so no choice is required

feedback.note: A purpose ranks other values. It does not wipe them out, freeze them forever, or remove the need to choose.

exercises.prompt: State what is missing when there is no purpose.

feedback.note: Values still exist as possibilities, but without a central goal they do not form a hierarchy one can act on.

exercises.prompt: Who chooses a person's purpose?

choices.text: The person, by a judgment of his own life
A crowd, by applause
A fate that thinking cannot touch
Nobody, because purposes are not chosen

feedback.note: A purpose is a choice. Applause and fate can pressure a person, but they do not do the choosing for him.

exercises.prompt: Match each case to whether it is a purpose.

pairs.left: Building a career one chose and can explain
Waiting to be told what is worth doing
Letting today's mood pick every goal

feedback.note: A purpose is a goal one chose and can stand behind. Waiting and drifting leave that choice unmade.

exercises.prompt: What is wrong with a purpose chosen against the facts?

choices.text: It is not a rational purpose, because a goal has to fit reality
It is better, because facts only limit small people
Nothing, because any intense wish counts as purpose
It becomes noble precisely by ignoring reality

feedback.note: Purpose depends on reason. A goal that contradicts the facts is a wish, not a rational purpose.

lessons.title: Self-esteem
lessons.objective: Explain self-esteem as the earned conviction that one is competent to think and worthy of living.

exercises.prompt: Which pair states the two parts of self-esteem in this unit?

choices.text: Competent to think, and worthy of living
Famous to others, and feared by rivals
Cheerful today, and liked in a group
Born to a rank, and excused from effort

feedback.note: Self-esteem is about one's mind and one's right to one's own life. Fame, mood, and rank are different claims.

exercises.prompt: Where does self-esteem come from?

choices.text: It is earned by one's own thinking and action
It is a gift other people can hand over
It is assigned at birth and cannot change
It arrives by luck and needs no cause

feedback.note: Self-esteem is earned. No audience, birth rank, or streak of luck can deposit it in a mind that has not earned it.

exercises.prompt: Match each statement to what it expresses.

pairs.left: I can think and judge
My life is worth living
They applaud me, so I am good

feedback.note: Competence and worthiness are the two parts of self-esteem. Applause is someone else's noise, not that conviction.

exercises.prompt: Complete the definition of self-esteem.

parts.text: Self-esteem is the conviction that one is

feedback.note: The two words are competent and worthy. Fame and excuses do not fill either blank.

exercises.prompt: Which habit undercuts self-esteem?

choices.text: Faking what one knows and living by others' verdicts
Judging by the facts one can see
Doing work one chose and can stand behind
Correcting a mistake when one finds it

feedback.note: Faking and outsourcing one's verdict tell the mind it is not competent. Judging, working, and correcting do the opposite.

exercises.prompt: Say how self-esteem is gained.

feedback.note: An audience can clap or boo. Neither act deposits self-esteem. The conviction has to be earned.

exercises.prompt: Can self-esteem stand if a person refuses to think?

choices.text: No. The conviction would not be about a mind that works.
Yes. Refusing to think makes the conviction purer.
Yes, if enough people still offer praise.
Yes, whenever the mood feels confident.

feedback.note: Self-esteem is confidence in one's competence to think. Drop the thinking and the confidence has nothing real to rest on.

exercises.prompt: Match each practice to its effect on self-esteem.

pairs.left: Judging by the facts
Pretending to know what one does not
Seeking approval instead of the truth

feedback.note: Judging by facts practices the competence self-esteem names. Pretense and approval-seeking practice the opposite.

exercises.prompt: Tie self-esteem back to the first cardinal value.

tokens.text: because the conviction is about one's mind

feedback.note: Self-esteem does not replace reason and does not float free of facts. It is a verdict about a mind that uses reason.

lessons.title: One set
lessons.objective: Hold reason, purpose, and self-esteem as one set, and see how each depends on the other two.

exercises.prompt: Which dependence among the three is the right one?

choices.text: Reason makes a rational purpose possible, and achieving it supports self-esteem
Self-esteem invents the facts, and purpose cancels the need to think
Each value works alone and none needs the others
The crowd supplies all three if one stays popular

feedback.note: Reason is the base. A purpose uses it. Self-esteem is the conviction that follows from thinking and from achieving what one chose.

exercises.prompt: Match each cardinal value to its place in the set.

pairs.left: Reason
pairs.right: The base the other two rest on

pairs.left: Purpose
Self-esteem
pairs.right: The result of thinking and achieving

feedback.note: Base, direction, and result are three jobs inside one set. None of the three is a spare part.

exercises.prompt: Complete the line about the set.

feedback.note: The missing value is purpose, and the three stand or fall together. They do not survive as separate whims.

exercises.prompt: State what happens if one cardinal value is dropped.

feedback.note: Removing one does not strengthen the rest. Purpose without reason, or self-esteem without either, has nothing firm under it.

exercises.prompt: What is wrong with claiming self-esteem while refusing reason?

choices.text: The conviction would be unearned
Nothing, because confidence is finer without facts
Refusal of reason is required for real confidence
Nothing, if the refusal stays private

feedback.note: Self-esteem names competence to think. A refusal to think leaves the claim with no earned base.

exercises.prompt: A goal chosen against the facts is which of these?

choices.text: Not a rational purpose
The best kind of purpose
Proof of self-esteem by itself
A higher form of reason

feedback.note: A rational purpose has to fit reality. Defying the facts is not a higher purpose, a proof of esteem, or a better use of reason.

exercises.prompt: Match each life to the set it shows.

pairs.left: Thinks, chooses his work, and trusts his mind
Follows feelings, drifts, and seeks praise
Knows facts, keeps no goal, and calls that humility

feedback.note: The full set uses all three. Drift replaces them. Facts without a goal and without esteem leave two of the three out.

exercises.prompt: Which of these is not a cardinal value in this unit?

choices.text: Sacrifice of one's life to other people's needs
Reason
Purpose
Self-esteem

feedback.note: Sacrifice of one's life to others is not one of the three. The cardinal values are reason, purpose, and self-esteem.

exercises.prompt: Name the three cardinal values in order.

feedback.note: The set stays reason, purpose, and self-esteem. Faith, sacrifice, and raw feeling are not stand-ins for that set.

exercises.prompt: A person uses reason, holds a productive purpose, and has earned self-esteem. What does this unit call that?

choices.text: The three cardinal values, held together
Three optional hobbies
A moral failure
A lucky mood with no cause

feedback.note: Held together, the three are the cardinal values of this ethics. They are not hobbies, vices, or a causeless mood.
